How much light would an earlier witness see?

Choose a brightness and a source-to-witness distance. The model asks how much visible light a point emitter would need to send into a uniform cone for the witness to receive that flux. It calculates photons and energy at the past emitter, then divides by a user-selected channel efficiency to estimate the energy A.R.G.O. would have to supply.

Illustrative range only. Matthew's account supplies no measured magnitude.
Logarithmic control: 1 m to 10¹¹ m. A local Earth sighting should use the actual observer range.
Uniform top-hat cone; 180° means isotropic emission into 4π steradians.
Logarithmic control: 0.1 to about 600 seconds.
Scenario fraction of ship-supplied energy delivered as emitter energy; independent of the chronal kernel's field-amplitude transmission ηK.

Assumed visual band: 500–600 nm · reference wavelength for photon count: 550 nm

Flat spectral flux density across the band. No dust, atmosphere, gravitational redshift, or absorption.
Isolated-source recoil scenario, initially at rest. If the chronal field supplies energy or momentum during emission, include that field in the conservation ledger.
The recoil calculation assumes uniform power per solid angle inside an axisymmetric cone and no external support during the pulse.

fν = 3631 Jy × 10−0.4mAB;  Fband ≈ fνΔν,   Δν = c(1/λmin − 1/λmax).
Ω = 2π(1 − cos α);   Pemit = Fband R²Ω;   EA.R.G.O. = PemitΔt/ηE.
pγ = (Eemit/c)(1 + cos α)/2;   Mfc² = √[(Mc² − Eemit)² − (pγc)²].

For the default example (mAB=−2, 1 km, 10° cone, 10 s, 1% efficiency), output is about 2.2 mW and 22 mJ of visible light; the assumed ship-side supply is about 2.2 J.

Power grows with distance squared

The selected point assumes the same brightness and beam angle at every distance. For a fixed magnitude and beam, doubling range needs four times the output power.

What this calculation does: converts a stated apparent brightness into a conditional photon and energy budget using the AB magnitude convention. AB zero magnitude corresponds to 3631 Jy of spectral flux density (STScI reference). What remains unknown: the Star's true brightness and distance, whether the historical light was a point source, the source spectrum, the photon path through the chronology-changing geometry, and whether a past emitter can receive the required energy. A.R.G.O. still needs a continuous channel solution before this optical budget can be called a mission result.
